ety.text: Verb from Middle English liken, from Old English līcian (“to like, to please”), from Proto-West Germanic *līkēn, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“image; likeness; similarity”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian liekje (“to be similar, resemble”), West Frisian lykje (“to seem, appear, look”), Dutch lijken (“to seem”), Low German lieken (“to be like; resemble”), German gleichen (“to resemble”), Swedish lika (“to like; put up with; align with”), Norwegian like (“to like”), Icelandic and Faroese líka (“to like”).

Adjective from Middle English lik, lyk, lich, like, from Old English ġelīċ by shortening, influenced by Old Norse líkr, glíkr; both from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz (“like, similar, same”). Related to alike; more distantly, with lich and -ly.
From like (adverb) and like (adjective).

senses.d: To enjoy, be pleased by; favor; be in favor of.
ex: I like reading books.
I very much like hamburgers.

senses.d: To please (same meaning as above but with subject and object reversed).
ex: His countenance likes me not.

senses.d: To derive pleasure [with of or by or with ‘from someone or something’].
To prefer and maintain (an action) as a regular habit or activity.
ex: I like to go to the dentist every six months.
She likes to keep herself physically fit.

senses.d: To find attractive; to prefer the company of; to have mild romantic feelings for.
ex: I really like Sandra but don't know how to tell her.
― Enju: “Apparently when you like someone, you start talking like them.”

senses.d: To want, desire. See also would like.
ex: Would you like a cigarette?
We could go to the museum if you like.

senses.d: To show support for, or approval of, something posted on the Internet by marking it with a vote.
ex: I liked my friend's last status on Facebook.
I can't stand Bloggs' tomato ketchup, but I liked it on Facebook so I could enter a competition.
Too bad this cheese likes to stick to the pan and ruin the whole meal.

senses.d: Of a computer or other system: to tolerate as an input; to accept.
ex: This self-service checkout doesn't seem to like my credit card.
We were frustrated that our seeming innocent choice for a team name was rejected by the game. Apparently somewhere in the name is a word that the algorithm doesn’t like.

senses.d: To come near; to avoid with difficulty; to escape narrowly.
ex: He liked to have been too late.
